title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope Targets August 30 Launch, Will Double as Asteroid Hunter
excerpt: The most powerful survey telescope ever built enters final prelaunch work at Kennedy Space Center, nine months ahead of schedule, with capabilities spanning dark energy research to planetary defense.
body:
• NASA targets August 30 for Roman Space Telescope launch aboard SpaceX Falcon Heavy, nine months ahead of the original May 2027 deadline
  • The observatory will carry a 300-megapixel infrared camera with a field of view 100 times larger than Hubble, enabling it to survey billions of galaxies, exoplanets, and near-Earth asteroids
  • Roman will join the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and the upcoming NEO Surveyor mission to form a three-telescope planetary defense network
  • The mission is expected to amass a 20,000-terabyte data archive over its five-year primary mission, enabling study of 100,000 exoplanets

Final Preparations at Kennedy Space Center

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has entered its final stretch of prelaunch work at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with the agency and SpaceX targeting a launch date of August 30, 2026 — nine months ahead of the original May 2027 commitment.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ZGQGv6d6uYk

Engineers raised the observatory from horizontal to vertical in early July after it arrived at Kennedy aboard NASA's Pegasus barge on June 21. The telescope is now undergoing inspections, functional testing, and integration work inside the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility.

"Roman's accelerated development is a true success story of what we can achieve when public investment, institutional expertise, and private enterprise come together to take on the near-impossible missions that change the world."

— Jared Isaacman, NASA Administrator

A Wide-Angle Eye on the Universe

Named after Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer and the "mother of the Hubble Space Telescope," the observatory is built around a 2.4-meter primary mirror originally donated by the National Reconnaissance Office. Its Wide-Field Instrument — a 300.8-megapixel multi-band visible and near-infrared camera — offers resolution comparable to Hubble's but spans a field of view 100 times larger.

That panoramic capability will allow Roman to survey vast stretches of sky in a single observation. Over its five-year primary mission, the telescope is expected to build a 20,000-terabyte data archive covering 100,000 exoplanets, hundreds of millions of galaxies, and billions of stars.

A separate Coronagraph Instrument will directly image exoplanets and planet-forming disks by blocking out the blinding light of host stars — a technology demonstration that could shape the design of future missions.

Earth's Newest Asteroid Hunter

While Roman was designed primarily to study dark energy, dark matter, and exoplanets, its infrared sensitivity makes it a powerful tool for planetary defense. Positioned at the Earth-Sun L2 Lagrange point, about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, the telescope will study near-Earth objects — asteroids and comets whose orbits bring them close to our planet.

Unlike telescopes that simply detect asteroids, Roman can determine their size, shape, composition, and precise orbital paths, according to NASA. That level of detail is critical for distinguishing objects that pose genuine threats from those that will safely pass by.

Roman will not work alone. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, already operational in Chile, uses visible light to scan the sky and is expected to discover more than 100,000 new near-Earth objects. The upcoming NEO Surveyor space mission will observe in mid-infrared wavelengths, potentially detecting between 200,000 and 300,000 NEOs, some as small as 20 meters across.

What's Next

The telescope will launch on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center. NASA and SpaceX have said they will share a specific launch date as prelaunch preparations continue.

The mission is managed at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, with support from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Caltech/IPAC, and the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore. Roman's construction was completed on November 25, 2025, and the telescope carries a plaque bearing the names of 1.3 million members of the public who signed up to have their names sent into space.
